## Setup

Ensure the work happens in an isolated workspace: use
superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one.
Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
partner's explicit consent.

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. An inline executor that
loses its place re-implements tasks whose commits already exist — the same
failure as a controller re-dispatching them, paid for in your own context.
Track progress in a ledger file, not only in todos. Harness todos are a
live view; the ledger is the record.

The workspace and ledger are shared with superpowers:subagent-driven-development
— same directory, same format — so a plan can change executors mid-flight
and the new one resumes from the same ledger.

- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run
  `../subagent-driven-development/scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` — it
  prints the plan's git-ignored directory
  (`<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/<plan-basename>/`), home to every
  artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, review packages. Another plan's
  directory is never yours to read or write.
- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If its first
  line names your plan file, tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are
  DONE — do not redo them; resume at the first task without one. Their
  commits exist in git even when your context no longer remembers making
  them: after compaction, trust the ledger and `git log` over your own
  recollection. A ledger whose first line names a different plan file is
  another plan's progress: leave it and start your own, fresh.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch);
  if that happens, recover from `git log`.

Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
todo per task. If the plan names a Spec, read that too: the spec is the
authority the plan argues from, and conflicts inside the plan resolve
against it. A plan with no reachable spec gets a ledger note saying so —
rulings made without one are provisional.

**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** load superpowers:test-driven-development now,
before Task 1. It governs every step of every task below; a plan whose
steps already say "write the failing test first" does not exempt you
from reading it.

Before Task 1, scan the plan for conflicts between tasks. The plan's
Interfaces blocks tell you where to look: for every task that consumes
what an earlier task produces, one ledger row — the two tasks, what one
produces against what the other consumes, and what you found. Tasks that
share nothing get no row; a plan whose tasks share nothing gets the single
line `Pre-flight: no shared interfaces`. Rule on each conflict a row
surfaces with the spec as the binding authority, record the ruling beside
its row, and start Task 1. Each task's own text is checked when you read
its brief, not here.

## The Task Loop

Everything you print, and every tool result, stays resident in your
context for the rest of the session. Redirect long test output to a file
in the workspace and read its tail; read a brief, not the whole plan.

### 1. Take the task

- Run this skill's `scripts/task-start PLAN_FILE N`. It prints the brief
  path and BASE (the commit the task's range is cut from) in one call.
  Read the brief for every task, including ones you remember from setup:
  what you remember is a summary, the brief has the exact values,
  signatures, and test cases.
- Mark the task's todo in_progress.

Every tool call is a turn that re-reads your whole context. Bookkeeping
rides along with work — a ledger append in the same call as the commit,
never in a call of its own.

### 2. Work the steps

The plan's steps are already in RED-GREEN order; follow them in that
order under superpowers:test-driven-development, loaded at setup. A test
step's code is written first and run first. Watching it fail is a step,
not a formality — a test that passes before the implementation exists is
a finding about the test.

Every step that runs a command has an `Expected:` line. Run the command,
read its output, and compare. Three outcomes:

- **Matches.** Next step.
- **The code is wrong.** Use superpowers:systematic-debugging. Find the
  cause; never patch the symptom to make the step's output match.
- **The plan is wrong** — a step contradicts the spec, an interface from an
  earlier task doesn't match what this task consumes, a command that
  cannot work. Rule on the smallest change that satisfies the spec, ledger
  it as `Task <N>: Ruling: <finding> — <what you decided and why>`, and
  continue. The ruling is carried, not remembered: later tasks that touch
  the same interface read it from the ledger.

Commit as the plan's commit steps say. A task that spans several commits
is fine; BASE is what the review range is cut from, never `HEAD~1`.

### 3. The completion contract

Before a task's ledger line, all of the following are true, with evidence
in this session — not inferred from the diff looking right:

- Every test the brief names exists and ran in this task, and you read
  the output.
- The final test run for the task passed — `task-done` is that run, and
  it writes the command and result into the ledger line.
- Every `Expected:` line in the brief was compared against real output.
- Every deviation from the brief has a `Ruling:` line in the ledger.

**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** superpowers:verification-before-completion governs
the claim. If any item is missing, the task is not complete: finish it.

### 4. Complete the task

Run this skill's `scripts/task-done PLAN_FILE N BASE -- <test command>`
with the test command the brief names for the whole task. It runs the
tests, keeps the full output in the workspace, prints the tail, and — only
if they pass — appends the completion line to the ledger:

`Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, tests: <command> → <result>)`

A failing run records nothing; the task is not complete. When it records,
mark the todo complete and take the next task.

## Final Review

Run `../subagent-driven-development/scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD`
(MERGE_BASE = the commit the branch started from, e.g.
`git merge-base main HEAD`) and review from the file it prints.

**With a subagent tool:** dispatch the reviewer on the most capable
available model — the whole-branch review is a judgment task — using
superpowers:requesting-code-review's
[code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md), with the
package path, the plan and spec paths, the plan's Review Focus section
verbatim if it has one (the input classes and failure modes the plan's
tests do not exercise — the reviewer checks each deliberately), and a
pointer to the ledger's `Ruling:` lines so it can weigh the calls you
made. Specify the model
explicitly; an omitted model inherits the session's, which may not be the
most capable. This is the one fresh context the whole run buys. Do not
skip it, and do not replace it with your own read of the diff.

**Without a subagent tool:** read code-reviewer.md and perform that review
yourself against the package, as a separate pass after the last task's
ledger line. Write `Final review: self-review (no subagent tool)` to the
ledger, and say so in your final message: a self-review by the author is
weaker than a fresh reviewer, and your human partner decides whether that
is enough before merge.

Sort the findings before you act on any of them. The reviewer's severity
labels are advice; the gate is yours. Its "Declined to judge" list is
yours too: every line there is a ruling you make and ledger, exactly like
a plan conflict — `Final: Ruling: <behavior the reviewer set aside> —
<what a reasonable person using this software gets, and why that stands
or why it is now a finding> — <cost if wrong>`. Re-grade first, by effect: the
spec is a vision document, and a finding's grade is what a reasonable
person using this software gets if it ships, not whether the spec names
the input that triggers it — a reviewer who set a finding at Minor
because the spec was silent has graded the spec, not the effect. Then:

- **Critical and Important** enter the fix pass.
- **Minor** goes to the ledger as `Final: minor (deferred): <one-liner>`
  and to your final message under "Deferred minors". Minors never enter
  the fix pass, and never become rulings — a ruling is a decision about a
  conflict, not a note that you declined a polish suggestion.

Fix the Critical and Important findings yourself — you are the
implementer here — in ONE pass. Each fix is verified by TDD, not by a
second reviewer: write the test that reproduces the finding, watch it
fail, make it pass, then run the whole suite. Record each in the ledger as
`Final: fixed <finding> — <test name> RED→GREEN, suite <N>/<N>`. A fix
without a test that failed first is not verified; a suite that is not
green after the pass means the pass is not over. Do not dispatch a
re-review: it would re-read a diff whose covering tests already answer
"addressed" and whose suite run already answers "broke nothing".

A finding you decide not to fix is a ruling — `Final: Ruling: <finding> —
<why the code stands> — <cost if wrong>` — and reaches your human partner
in the rulings list. There is no second fix pass.

## Finish

Before you delete anything, collect every ledger line containing
`Ruling:` into your final message under "Rulings I made", in the order you
made them, each with what it costs if wrong, and every `minor (deferred)`
line under "Deferred minors". Both lists are exhaustive. Your final
message is the only place the decisions you took on your human partner's
behalf — and the findings you chose not to act on — reach them.

When the final review is clean and its fixes are committed, delete this
plan's workspace directory — the git history is the record now. Sibling
directories belong to other plans; leave them alone.

Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "I remember what Task N says" | You remember a summary. The brief has the exact values. Read it. |
| "The plan's code is right, skip watching the test fail" | A test you never saw fail proves nothing. It is one step. Run it. |
| "I'll run the full suite at the end instead of per step" | Per-step runs are how you learn which step broke it. The end-of-task run is the contract, not a substitute. |
| "The plan is wrong here, I'll just do the right thing" | Do the right thing and ledger the ruling. Unledgered deviation is a decision made in secret. |
| "I'll write the ledger lines after a few tasks" | Compaction does not wait for a convenient moment. One line per task, in the same message as the commit. |
| "Let me check in before the next task" | They chose inline to spend less. Progress prompts spend their time instead. Only the four stops stop you. |
| "I read my own diff carefully; the final reviewer is redundant" | Same author, same blind spots. The reviewer is the only fresh context this run buys. |
| "Tests should pass, the change was trivial" | "Should" is not evidence. The contract requires the command and its output. |
| "Subagents are slow and expensive, I'll skip the final review too" | Inline already removed the per-task reviewers. One review of the whole branch is the floor, not the ceiling. |
| "The reviewer said Minor, so it's Minor" | The label graded the spec's silence. Grade what the person gets. Re-grade, then gate. |
| "The fix is obvious, no need for a failing test first" | The failing test is the only proof the finding was real and is now gone. Without it you have a diff and a hope. |
| "I'll fix the minors too while I'm in there" | Every minor you fix is a test, a fix, and a suite run your partner did not ask for. Ledger them; your partner decides. |

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prints the release version, <minecraft_version>-<mod_version>, read from gradle.properties.
# The release tag and the jar name both use this version.
# Usage: release-version.sh [repo dir]
set -euo pipefail

repo="${1:-.}"

property() {
  awk -v key="$1" 'index($0, key "=") == 1 { print substr($0, length(key) + 2); exit }' "$repo/gradle.properties"
}

minecraft=$(property minecraft_version)
mod=$(property mod_version)
if [[ -z "$minecraft" || -z "$mod" ]]; then
  echo "gradle.properties in $repo needs both minecraft_version and mod_version" >&2
  exit 1
fi
printf '%s-%s\n' "$minecraft" "$mod"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prints the notes for one version from the changelog, which the release uses for GitHub, CurseForge and Modrinth.
# The notes are the lines under the "## <tag>" heading up to the next "## " heading, without the blank lines around them.
# Usage: changelog-section.sh <tag> [changelog file]
set -euo pipefail

tag="${1:?usage: changelog-section.sh <tag> [changelog file]}"
file="${2:-CHANGELOG.md}"

section=$(awk -v heading="## $tag" '
  $0 == heading { inside = 1; next }
  inside && /^## / { exit }
  inside && !started && /^[[:space:]]*$/ { next }
  inside { started = 1; print }
' "$file")

if [[ -z "$section" ]]; then
  echo "$file has no notes under \"## $tag\"" >&2
  exit 1
fi
printf '%s\n' "$section"

# Checks a release tag before anything is built or published: the tag must equal the version in gradle.properties,
# and the changelog must have notes for it. The release workflow and `just release-check` both run it.

if [[ "$tag" != "$expected" ]]; then
  echo "tag $tag does not match gradle.properties, which gives $expected" >&2
  exit 1
fi
bash "$tools/changelog-section.sh" "$tag" "$repo/CHANGELOG.md" > /dev/null
echo "$tag is ready to release"

Modular Planters is an addon for Agritech: Evolved that replaces rows of Advanced Planters with one multiblock. A Modular Planter Block grows up to 64 seeds, and every Modular Planter Block in the multiblock shares one power supply, one fertilizer supply and one output store.

Needs Minecraft 26.1.2, NeoForge 26.1.2.116 or newer, and Agritech: Evolved 2.2.0 or newer. Optional: AE2, Applied Flux, Jade, Oracle Index and Logistics Networks.

## Features

- One connection to the Modular Planter Core runs power, fertilizer and outputs
- The Modular Planter Core's screen lists every Modular Planter Block's seed, upgrades and status
- A built-in cloche that needs no item
- An optional Modular Planter ME Block for AE2, with Applied Flux power

  - `type`: `ALPHA` when `mod_version` ends with `-alpha`, `BETA` when it ends with `-beta`, otherwise `STABLE`.

on:

jobs:

    steps:

      - uses: actions/setup-java@v6
        with:

      - uses: j178/prek-action@44924fe9ef4a6f88253c4b6b1bf11c689d3ce53d # v3.1.0

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - uses: gradle/actions/setup-gradle@8da46b539cd8fe6ab27ca75128919a18d757604c # v6.4.1
      - run: ./gradlew runData
      - name: Check that the generated data is committed

name: Release

on:
  push:
    tags: ["*.*.*-*.*.*"]

permissions:
  contents: read

defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash

jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      curseforge: ${{ steps.projects.outputs.curseforge }}
      modrinth: ${{ steps.projects.outputs.modrinth }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: bash tools/check-release.sh "$GITHUB_REF_NAME"
      - name: Read the CurseForge and Modrinth project ids
        id: projects
        run: |
          for site in curseforge modrinth; do
            id=$(awk -F= -v key="${site}_project_id" '$1 == key { print $2 }' gradle.properties)
            if [ -z "$id" ]; then
              echo "::notice::${site}_project_id is empty in gradle.properties, so this release skips ${site}."
            fi
            echo "${site}=${id}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          done

  checks:
    needs: verify
    uses: ./.github/workflows/checks.yml

  github:
    needs: checks
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v6
        with:
          distribution: microsoft
          java-version: "25"
      - uses: gradle/actions/setup-gradle@8da46b539cd8fe6ab27ca75128919a18d757604c # v6.4.1
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          name: jar
          path: dist
      - run: ./gradlew publishGithub -PpublishJar="dist/modular_planters-${GITHUB_REF_NAME}.jar"
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

  curseforge:
    needs: [verify, checks]
    if: needs.verify.outputs.curseforge != ''
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v6
        with:
          distribution: microsoft
          java-version: "25"
      - uses: gradle/actions/setup-gradle@8da46b539cd8fe6ab27ca75128919a18d757604c # v6.4.1
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          name: jar
          path: dist
      - run: ./gradlew publishCurseforge -PpublishJar="dist/modular_planters-${GITHUB_REF_NAME}.jar"
        env:
          CURSEFORGE_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.CURSEFORGE_API_KEY }}

  modrinth:
    needs: [verify, checks]
    if: needs.verify.outputs.modrinth != ''
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v6
        with:
          distribution: microsoft
          java-version: "25"
      - uses: gradle/actions/setup-gradle@8da46b539cd8fe6ab27ca75128919a18d757604c # v6.4.1
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          name: jar
          path: dist
      - run: ./gradlew publishModrinth -PpublishJar="dist/modular_planters-${GITHUB_REF_NAME}.jar"
        env:
          MODRINTH_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.MODRINTH_API_KEY }}

# Local entry points for this repository. `just` lists them; `just <recipe>` runs one.
#
# CI does not call just: the pipeline runs the docker/build component, which drives
# `docker buildx bake` itself. The recipes here run the same commands so that a local
# build and a pipeline build resolve the same tags and arguments.

set shell := ["bash", "-euo", "pipefail", "-c"]

# Recipe arguments arrive as $1, $2, ... so variadic recipes forward them with "$@" and
# keep each argument intact.
set positional-arguments

# CI reads the sha from CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA. Locally it has to be supplied, or every
# build on one day resolves to the same tag. See build_id() in docker-bake.hcl.
export GIT_SHA := `git rev-parse --short=8 HEAD`

# A local build is never a release, so it publishes only the build id and can never
# overwrite a tag that a pipeline pushed.
export RELEASE := "false"

# https://docs.docker.com/build/building/variables/#buildx_git_info
export BUILDX_GIT_INFO := "1"
export BUILDX_GIT_LABELS := "full"

[private]
default:
    @just --list --unsorted

# Local shortcuts for building, testing, formatting and releasing Modular Planters. `just` lists them, and `just <recipe>` runs one.
#
# CI does not call just. The workflows in .github/workflows run the same Gradle tasks and tools/ scripts directly.

set shell := ["bash", "-euo", "pipefail", "-c"]

# Recipe arguments arrive as $1, $2 and so on, so variadic recipes forward them with "$@" and keep each argument intact.
set positional-arguments

[private]
default:
    @just --list --unsorted

[doc('Compile, run the unit tests and build the jar into build/libs/')]
[group('gradle')]
build:
    ./gradlew build

[doc('Run the unit tests in src/test')]
[group('gradle')]
test:
    ./gradlew test

[doc('Run the in-game tests on a headless server, for example: just gametest -PnoAe2')]
[group('gradle')]
gametest *flags:
    ./gradlew runGameTestServer "$@"

[doc('Run the unit tests, then the in-game tests with all dev mods, without AE2 and without Applied Flux, like CI does')]
[group('gradle')]
check:
    ./gradlew test
    ./gradlew runGameTestServer
    ./gradlew runGameTestServer -PnoAe2
    ./gradlew runGameTestServer -PnoAppliedFlux

[doc('Start a dev client, for example: just client -PnoPowah')]
[group('gradle')]
client *flags:
    ./gradlew runClient "$@"

[doc('Start a dev dedicated server')]
[group('gradle')]
server *flags:
    ./gradlew runServer "$@"

[doc('Regenerate src/generated/resources')]
[group('gradle')]
data:
    ./gradlew runData

[doc('Run every pre-commit hook on every file, as CI does')]
[group('lint')]
lint:
    prek run --all-files --show-diff-on-failure

# The formatters exit 1 when they rewrite a file, so a second run decides the result: it passes when the first run fixed everything.
[doc('Format the Java, Markdown, YAML and JSON files in place')]
[group('lint')]
fmt:
    prek run --all-files pretty-format-java prettier || prek run --all-files pretty-format-java prettier

[doc('Render the mod logo into docs/media/logo.png and src/main/resources/logo.png')]
[group('media')]
logo:
    uv run tools/render_logo.py

[doc('Compress PNG files in place, for example: just compress docs/media/*.png')]
[group('media')]
compress +files:
    pngquant --quality=80-95 --speed 1 --strip --force --ext .png "$@"
    oxipng -o 4 --strip safe "$@"

[doc('Print the changelog notes for one release tag, for example: just changelog 26.1.2-0.1.0')]
[group('release')]
changelog version:
    bash tools/changelog-section.sh "$1"

[doc('Check that the version in gradle.properties is ready to tag, then dry-run the publish to GitHub, CurseForge and Modrinth')]
[group('release')]
release-check:
    bash tools/check-release.sh "$(bash tools/release-version.sh)"
    DRY_RUN=1 GITHUB_TOKEN=REDACTED ./gradlew publishMods

# Developing Modular Planters

## Setup

- A JDK 17 or newer on your `PATH` or in `JAVA_HOME`, to start Gradle 9.2.1 through the wrapper (`./gradlew`).
- The build compiles and runs with JDK 25. Gradle finds an installed JDK 25 or downloads one through the Foojay toolchain resolver, so installing JDK 25 yourself covers both needs.
- An IDE is optional. IntelliJ IDEA imports the project from `build.gradle`, and the `idea` plugin downloads sources and javadoc for Minecraft and NeoForge.

The first build downloads Minecraft, NeoForge and the dev mods, so it takes a few minutes.

## Gradle tasks

| Command                       | What it does                                                                                   |
| ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `./gradlew build`             | Compiles, runs the unit tests and builds the jar into `build/libs/`                            |
| `./gradlew test`              | Runs the unit tests in `src/test`                                                              |
| `./gradlew runGameTestServer` | Starts a headless server that runs the in-game tests in `src/main/java/.../gametest` and exits |
| `./gradlew runClient`         | Starts a dev client with the mod and the dev mods below                                        |
| `./gradlew runServer`         | Starts a dev dedicated server with no GUI                                                      |
| `./gradlew runData`           | Regenerates `src/generated/resources` (recipes, loot tables, lang, models)                     |

Run `./gradlew test` and `./gradlew runGameTestServer` before opening a pull request.

## Where things live

- `src/main/java`: the mod. The `gametest` and `datagen` packages are left out of the jar.
- `src/generated/resources`: output of `runData`. It is committed, so run `runData` and commit the result after changing anything in `datagen`.
- `wiki/`: the guide's pages. `processResources` copies them into the jar, where Oracle Index reads them as a book.
- `docs/description.md` and `docs/media/`: the CurseForge and Modrinth page and its images. World shots are JPEG. Screenshots of screens are PNG, compressed with `pngquant --quality=80-95 --speed 1 --strip --force --ext .png <files>` and then `oxipng -o 4 --strip safe <files>` (`brew install pngquant oxipng`). The logo PNGs are left as `tools/render_logo.py` writes them.
- `tools/render_logo.py`: draws the logo from the block textures. Run `uv run tools/render_logo.py` after changing a block texture, and commit both `docs/media/logo.png` and `src/main/resources/logo.png`.

## Dev mods

These are on the dev runtime (`runClient`, `runServer`, `runGameTestServer`) but not in the jar. Agritech: Evolved is the only required dependency. Each switch below leaves a mod out of a run, for example `./gradlew runClient -PnoAe2`.

| Mod                | Version       | Comes with                     | Switch                                     |
| ------------------ | ------------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------ |
| Agritech: Evolved  | 2.2.0.6       |                                | required                                   |
| Jade               | 26.1.12       |                                | `-PnoJade`                                 |
| AE2                | 26.1.13-beta  | GuideME 26.1.15-beta           | `-PnoAe2`                                  |
| Applied Flux       | 26.1-1.0.2    | Glodium 26.1-1.2               | `-PnoAppliedFlux`, also off with `-PnoAe2` |
| Powah              | 7.0.4-alpha   | Cloth Config 26.1.154, GuideME | `-PnoPowah`                                |
| Oracle Index       | 2.0.0         | Architectury 20.1.17           | `-PnoOracleIndex`                          |
| Logistics Networks | 26.1.2-1.13.0 |                                | `-PnoLogisticsNetworks`                    |

The mod has code only for Jade, AE2 and Applied Flux. Powah is there for its fast FE source and cables. Oracle Index shows the guide, and Logistics Networks lets you test a node on the core. Most versions match the ones the All the Mods 11 modpack runs. Applied Flux isn't in that pack, and its AE2 build can differ.

## Screenshots with Structure Lab

`-PstructureLabJar=<path to jar>` adds Structure Lab to a dev run. It places a structure file in a flat world and saves screenshots from set camera angles, which is how the world shots in `docs/media/` were taken. It is a local build that isn't published, so leave the switch out unless you have the jar. It needs a world created with the "Structure Lab" world type.

# Contributing to Modular Planters

Contributions are welcome: bug fixes, compatibility fixes, guide corrections and code improvements.

I have a specific vision for the mod and what content fits it. Before working on new content or a balance change, please open an issue and talk it through first, so your time isn't spent on something that won't be merged.

## Issues

- Search the open and closed issues first. Your bug or idea may already be there.
- Use the bug report or feature request form. For bugs, a log link and steps to reproduce make the biggest difference.

## Pull requests

- Make one pull request per change. Separate fixes are easier to review and to revert.
- Link the issue the pull request fixes.
- Say how you tested it. At least run `./gradlew test` and `./gradlew runGameTestServer`, and check client-side changes in game and on a dedicated server.
- Check your spelling and grammar in text players see, such as the guide in `wiki/` and the lang entries.

[DEVELOPMENT.md](DEVELOPMENT.md) explains how to set up the project and run it locally.

| `just changelog <tag>`  | Prints the changelog notes for one release                                                     |

## Releasing

# Code Reviewer Prompt Template

Use this template when dispatching a code reviewer subagent.

**Purpose:** Review completed work against requirements and code quality standards before it cascades into more work.

```
Subagent (general-purpose):
  description: "Review code changes"
  prompt: |
    You are a Senior Code Reviewer with expertise in software architecture,
    design patterns, and best practices. Your job is to review completed work
    against its plan or requirements and identify issues before they cascade.

    ## What Was Implemented

    [DESCRIPTION]

    ## Requirements / Plan

    [PLAN_OR_REQUIREMENTS]

    ## Git Range to Review

    **Base:** [BASE_SHA]
    **Head:** [HEAD_SHA]

    ```bash
    git diff --stat [BASE_SHA]..[HEAD_SHA]
    git diff [BASE_SHA]..[HEAD_SHA]
    ```

    ## The spec is a vision document

    The spec says what the software must do. It does not enumerate every
    input, environment, or condition the software will meet. For behavior
    the spec is silent on, judge by what a reasonable person using this
    software would expect: a reasonable person's expectation is a
    requirement, and a spec's silence is not permission. Grade such
    findings by their effect on that person, not by whether the spec
    mentions the trigger.

    ## Declined to judge

    Before your verdict, list every behavior you considered and set aside
    as outside the plan or spec, one line each, with the reason. The
    executor rules on each line; nothing you set aside is dropped
    silently. An empty list means you set nothing aside.

    ## Read-Only Review

    Your review is read-only on this checkout. Do not mutate the working tree, the index, HEAD, or branch state in any way. Use tools like `git show`, `git diff`, and `git log` to inspect history. If you need a working copy of a different revision, check it out into a separate temporary directory (e.g. `git worktree add /tmp/review-[SHA] [SHA]`) — never move HEAD on this checkout.

    ## You Do Not Dispatch Subagents

    Do all of this review yourself. Never spawn a subagent to review part
    of the diff, and never spawn another reviewer for a second opinion.
    This process already provides every review seat the work gets; a
    reviewer you spawn duplicates one of them at full cost, and its
    verdict counts for nothing. If the diff feels too large for one
    pass, review it in passes yourself and say so in your report.

    ## What to Check

    **Plan alignment:**
    - Does the implementation match the plan / requirements?
    - Are deviations justified improvements, or problematic departures?
    - Is all planned functionality present?

    **Code quality:**
    - Clean separation of concerns?
    - Proper error handling?
    - Type safety where applicable?
    - DRY without premature abstraction?
    - Edge cases handled?

    **Architecture:**
    - Sound design decisions?
    - Reasonable scalability and performance?
    - Security concerns?
    - Integrates cleanly with surrounding code?

# Checks a release tag before anything is built or published: the tag must have the release format, equal the version
# in gradle.properties, and have notes in the changelog. The release workflow and `just release-check` both run it.
# Usage: check-release.sh <tag> [repo dir]
set -euo pipefail

tag="${1:?usage: check-release.sh <tag> [repo dir]}"
repo="${2:-.}"
tools=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)

# The tag is <minecraft version>-<mod version>, such as 26.1.2-0.1.0 or 26.3-0.2.0-beta.
# Every tag of this shape matches the release workflow's trigger, and the build only knows the -alpha and -beta suffixes,
# so any other suffix would publish as a full release.
format='^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?-[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+(-(alpha|beta)(\.[0-9]+)?)?$'
if [[ ! "$tag" =~ $format ]]; then
  echo "tag $tag is not <minecraft version>-<mod version>, where the mod version is three numbers with an optional -alpha or -beta suffix" >&2
  exit 1
fi

expected=$(bash "$tools/release-version.sh" "$repo")

**What's in it:**
- **Release naming:** releases are tagged and named `26.1.2-0.1.0`. `CHANGELOG.md` has one section per version.
- **Release scripts:** the scripts in `tools/` check the tag format, that it matches `gradle.properties`, and that the changelog has notes for it.
- **Publishing:** mod-publish-plugin publishes the jar the checks built to GitHub, then CurseForge and Modrinth. A site is skipped while its project id is empty.
- **Formatting:** prek runs google-java-format and Prettier, plus an `.editorconfig`. The whole codebase was reformatted in one commit, which `.git-blame-ignore-revs` hides from blame.
- **Workflows and justfile:** a build workflow runs on every push and pull request, and a release workflow runs on a tag. The justfile wraps it all, and the docs are updated.

**The reviewer (Opus) found nothing critical. I fixed:**
- **Tag pattern:** tags like `26.3-0.2.0` would never have started a release. Tags with a two-part Minecraft version now work. The release check now also rejects malformed versions, such as a two-number mod version or an `-rc1` suffix, which would otherwise have published as full releases.
- **setup-gradle licence:** v6 accepts a proprietary licence for its caching component on your behalf. It's back on v5.0.2, as the plan had it, so moving to v6 is your call.
- **Publish order:** CurseForge and Modrinth now wait for the GitHub release, as the spec says.
- **Comments and docs:** fixed a wrong comment in `build.gradle` and doc lines that overstated what `just check` covers. JSON in `.editorconfig` is now `unset`, matching "JSON can skip the rule".

**The side agent's merge warning is right:** merge this branch with a fast-forward or a merge commit, never squash or rebase. Otherwise `.git-blame-ignore-revs` points at a commit that isn't on `main`. Option 1 below is a fast-forward.

**Rulings I made:**
1. I worked on the branch in the main checkout, without a worktree. Cost if wrong: none.
2. The release script rejection tests expect exit 1. At first they passed while the scripts didn't exist yet (exit 127). Cost: none.
3. I added `tools/release-version.sh` so every caller reads the version the same way. Cost: one extra file.
4. From the first side agent: the test task now tracks `tools/` and the docs, so `./gradlew test` reruns after a script edit instead of reporting a stale pass. Cost: extra test reruns.
5. Alpha or beta is detected with "contains", so `0.2.0-beta.2` still publishes as a beta. Cost: none.
6. The release display name is "Modular Planters 26.1.2-0.1.0". The default was "ModularPlanters". Cost: one line.
7. The dry run doesn't print the release type, so that is unverified until the first real release.
8. google-java-format is pinned to 1.37.0, the latest 1.x. Cost: one argument.
9. Prettier skips `.claude/`, `.entire/`, `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`, because those tools rewrite the files. Cost: those files stay unformatted.
10. `.editorconfig` trims trailing whitespace to match the hook. Cost: one line.
11. The plan said all three GameTest runs print 126. The real counts are 126, 116 and 124, the same before and after the reformat. Cost: none.
12. Prettier moved the pull request template's "Remove the next line" comment off the line it meant, so I reworded it in its own commit. Cost: none.
13. Actions use their current major versions. Third-party actions are pinned by SHA. Cost: version bumps.
14. The CI prek job installs JDK 25 so google-java-format can read the code. Cost: one step.
15. The GameTest check matches "All N required tests passed", because the log line ends with " :)". Cost: none.
16. An empty project id shows up as a skipped job plus a notice. Cost: none.
17. `just fmt` runs the formatters a second time when the first run changed files. Cost: one extra run.
18. `just changelog` prints only the notes. Cost: none.
19. The setup docs ask for JDK 25 on your PATH, because the formatter hook uses that JDK. Cost: a stricter setup line than needed.
20. I left the reviewer's "declined to judge" items as they were. Most would fail visibly on the first release run, for example the CurseForge slugs and version names. Cost: a fix release.

# Defuddle

Use Defuddle CLI to extract clean readable content from web pages. Prefer over WebFetch for standard web pages — it removes navigation, ads, and clutter, reducing token usage.

If not installed: `npm install -g defuddle`

## Usage

Always use `--md` for markdown output:

```bash
defuddle parse <url> --md

Save to file:

```bash
defuddle parse <url> --md -o content.md

Extract specific metadata:

```bash
defuddle parse <url> -p title
defuddle parse <url> -p description
defuddle parse <url> -p domain
```

content.text:
You can close that dialog without uploading anything. Modrinth only needs a version before you submit the draft for review. The release workflow is built to upload that version, so the jar on Modrinth will be the same one CI builds for the GitHub release.

The first Build run on `main` passed: prek, generated data, the jar build and all three GameTest runs (2m40s).

What's left on Modrinth:
1. **Copy the project ID** from the project page. It's the 8-character ID, not the slug, because the plugin's example uses the ID. Paste it here or put it in `modrinth_project_id` in `gradle.properties`.
2. **Create a personal access token** at https://modrinth.com/settings/pats with the scopes Create versions, Read versions and Write versions. Those are the three the plugin's docs list. It doesn't need the project scopes, because we don't set `projectDescription`.
3. **Add the token as a GitHub secret** named `MODRINTH_API_KEY`: run `gh secret set MODRINTH_API_KEY`, or use the repo's Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions.

Do the same on CurseForge: get the project ID and add an API token as `CURSEFORGE_API_KEY`. Then I'll commit both IDs and push.

After that, you run `just release-check` and push the `26.1.2-0.1.0` tag. The release workflow reads the IDs from `gradle.properties` at the tagged commit, so the tag has to come after the ID commit. Once the workflow has uploaded the version, you submit the Modrinth draft for review.

If you upload a jar by hand here instead, the workflow would upload `26.1.2-0.1.0` a second time when you tag. To avoid that, the Modrinth ID would have to stay empty until after the first release.

=== https://support.modrinth.com/en/articles/16551575
Since [August 13th 2026](https://modrinth.com/news/article/ai-policy-and-disclosures/), we've implemented several requirements and restrictions on the use of generative AI ([LLMs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_language_model) and [TTI models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Text-to-image_model)) to our [Content Rules](https://modrinth.com/legal/rules).

We aim to make browsing Modrinth welcoming and easy, and ensure that human passion always has a place on our platform. To achieve this, we expect creators to be honest about their use of generative AI, and will not permit the upload of content that is entirely or primarily AI-generated.

**This does not pertain to mob AI used by entities, such as [pathfinding and brains](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Mob_AI), or scripts such as [data generation](https://docs.fabricmc.net/develop/data-generation/setup). These policies target content (code and assets) created using generative AI.**

## Transparency and Content Disclosures

We expect creators to be honest about the use of generative AI, as required by section 6.1 of Modrinth's Content Rules.

## Excerpt of Section 6.1

You must apply the appropriate “Contains AI-generated content” content disclosure when:

1. a substantial portion of the project's code is a product of AI output.
2. the project includes any assets that are primarily or entirely a product of AI output.
3. the project's design or functionality relies on the use of generative AI.
4. any element of the project's page such as description or publishing relies on generative AI.

## What makes for a "substantial portion" of the project?

If AI has played a notable role in creating or publishing your content, it's important that users are aware of that, and we ask that you do not attempt to hide the nature of your content from users.  

*A good rule of thumb is to ask yourself, "if a human was in place of the AI tool, would they expect to be credited?"*

ℹ️ This is a simple analogy meant to demonstrate our expectations of transparency and honesty from creators, and should not be taken to mean that AI output is similar or equivalent to human contribution, it is not.

For non-significant contributions, such as answering simple questions, reviewing code, checking grammar, refactoring a few functions, or filling in minor gaps for you, the answer is likely no. But if generative AI has generated assets, entire classes, translations, written your description, contributed a significant amount of content, or AI-generated output is the basis for your project, you must disclose how it has been used.

If the answer instead reveals that generative AI has played a role in your content worthy of being the primary developer, artist, or author, [your content may not be suitable for Modrinth](#h_7742ce5739).

[Read here for more information on content disclosures](https://support.modrinth.com/en/articles/16567675-modrinth-s-content-disclosures#h_acc3391fca).

## AI-generated Images

**Primarily or fully AI-generated images may not be uploaded to any part of your Modrinth project page**. This includes the project icon, gallery images, changelog, and description.  

Modrinth may reject the upload of your image if the use of generative AI, including any edits using generative AI, is detected. Attempting to bypass this restriction to upload AI-generated content may result in the removal of images or account suspension.  

### Deceptive Images

While any use of deceptive editing to give a false impression of your content is strictly prohibited, AI-generated or AI-assisted images are inherently the most guilty of this and should never be used to replace screenshots or any other demonstration of in-game content.  

### AI Icons and branding images

**The use of AI images for non-representative media such as icons, banners, and other branding assets is also prohibited.**

While this may feel like a cheap shortcut to creating an icon for your projects, we've found that AI images are overwhelmingly unpopular in any context. It's expected that a crude photobash, a sloppy drawing made in Microsoft Paint, or no icon at all will perform better than an AI-generated icon!

## Entirely AI-generated Projects

**Any project that is created entirely or almost entirely through the use of generative AI with little-to-no human input beyond prompting or testing cannot be published on Modrinth publicly.**

Projects generated by AI pose several risks to our community and our users, and are not what our users come to and know Modrinth for.  

## Ok, but what projects really?

Content that makes heavy use of generative AI in specific portions of a project may still be permitted if genuine human code/assets/writing makes up a significant portion of the project in another portion, so long as you are [honest with your users about your usage of AI](#h_b09611356b).

This regulation specifically targets projects that are created purely through "prompting and testing" with minimal or no real human-made content.

## What happens to AI projects?

In most cases, such projects can still be made unlisted, but will be prohibited from appearing in public search results. We ask that you keep this in mind before attempting to publish any AI-generated content to Modrinth.

## Forking content with AI

Modrinth aims to protect the community-driven and open-source nature of Minecraft projects. Regardless of generative AI's role, every project must abide by our [content rules](https://modrinth.com/legal/rules) regarding creating sufficiently divergent forks.

We know that most creators are not comfortable with forks such as version or loader ports being mass-produced by users running their project through generative AI.

For this reason, forks are judged based on the original content added upon the source work. This means that a fork's "original" content may be prohibited from publication if it is [primarily or entirely AI-generated](#h_2e46215d9f), even if the source work does not make significant use of generative AI.

## Disclosing AI usage in forked content

If a project you're forking makes substantial use of generative AI, **we ask that you maintain disclosure of this use**, unless your fork has removed all AI-generated content. You are welcome to clarify that AI-generated content is present in the source work if not added by yourself.

Likewise, if you have made substantial use of generative AI in your fork, but the source work does not, **you will be required to clarify that AI-generated content is not present in the source work**.

## What about "slop" or non-AI projects?

While concerns about the quality of content that generative AI currently produces do play a minor role, it is not the primary motivator for our regulations on AI-generated content.

Creators are welcome and encouraged to publish "bad" *(subjective!)* projects on Modrinth. Not only because everyone starts from somewhere, but also because being inclusive and welcoming everyone of every skill level is what makes up our community.

**Using tools such as project templates or MCreator to help you get started on that journey, or to take you all the way to a million downloads, is welcome.**

## Then why AI specifically?

Generative AI has ethical, economic, and ecological concerns that we believe users deserve to be informed of if they cut AI-generated content out of their modding diet.

These concerns are elevated for fully AI-generated projects, which can be produced rapidly with extractive intent, without ever understanding our community or what makes modding so special.

**These concerns are present whenever generative AI has been used in the production or publication of a project, even if that content may be subjectively "good."**

## Does the use of AI impact a project's Monetization?

Disclosing the usage of generative AI in your project has no negative impact on your project's place in search results or revenue. Please refer to our [Rewards Program Information](https://modrinth.com/legal/cmp-info) page for more details.

=== https://modrinth.com/news/article/ai-policy-and-disclosures/
An update to Modrinth’s Content Rules and our new mandatory content disclosures.

[Modrinth Team](https://modrinth.com/organization/modrinth) •August 13, 2026

This year, fully AI-generated content has begun *flooding* Modrinth. Project submissions have gone up from about 2,500 per week at the start of the year to over 5,000 per week now.

We’ve never had a quality threshold for uploading to Modrinth, and we continue to believe that you should not need to make professional, perfect work in order to publish on Modrinth. But we do believe that it has to be *your* work, and generating it completely with AI is not your work. Modrinth is a community of creators. In order to be creators, you need to actually create something.

Today, we’re announcing a set of new features and policies aimed at informing users about things they may want to know about a project before downloading, eliminating fully AI-generated content, and enforcing transparency for content that has been made in part with generative AI.

In addition, we have made a very minor update to our [Terms of Use](https://modrinth.com/legal/terms), to prohibit the use of data on Modrinth to train AI models.

## Content disclosures

We have introduced content disclosures to provide a standardized place for certain things that we feel it is important for users to understand before downloading a project on Modrinth.

![In the Details panel on the sidebar of a project, a couple disclosures are listed as an example. Contains paid features: Cosmetic items are purchaseable with Mod Coins; Contains opt-out telemetry: Anonymous launch analytics about game version and mod loaders.](https://modrinth.com/news/article/ai-policy-and-disclosures/details.webp)

Here’s the current list of content disclosures available at this time:

- **Contains AI-generated content**
	- Projects must enable this if they:
		- contain a substantial amount of AI-generated code
				- *any* assets that are substantially AI-generated
				- the project’s functionality relies on the use of generative AI
				- or, if any element of your project’s page such as description or publishing relies on generative AI
		- There are also options available to disclose if you use it for code, assets, text, or functionality within the project.
- **Contains advertising**
	- Projects that contain advertisements, sponsorships, or promotions of other works must enable this disclosure.
		- If the promotion has no direct monetary value ***and*** it is for something that the average person would consider *relevant* and *unobtrusive* (such as a link to your Modrinth profile in the corner of the settings page for your own mod), we would not consider that an advertisement for the purposes of this disclosure.
- **Contains paid features**
	- Projects that contain features that can be obtained by spending real-world money.
		- You must provide a list of the types of paid features.
- **Contains telemetry**
	- If your project collects any data on users (sent either to yourself or a third party), it must be disclosed here.
		- There’s three types of telemetry consent options you can select: Opt-in, Opt-out, and Always active
		- You must provide a list of the types of data that is collected.
- **Contains derivative content**
	- If your project is a fork or uses substantial parts of another work, you must declare it as a derivative work of the source work.
		- You must at least provide the name of the work, and if available, a link. You may also provide a small explanation of how it is a derivative work, such as a brief summary of what is different about your fork.
- **Photosensitivity warning**
	- If your project contains anything that you think may be dangerous to certain people who are sensitive to flashing lights or patterns, you must enable the photosensitivity disclosure.
- **Contains external system interactions**
	- Projects that read or edit things on the user’s system outside of the game must enable this disclosure.
		- You must describe precisely how it interacts with the user’s system in the required note.
		- The most common usage of this is in some “horror” mods, where they may do harmless but spooky things on your computer such as adding creepy files to your desktop.
- **Archived**
	- This isn’t new, but we’re transitioning it from a project visibility status to a disclosure.
		- This will allow you to have an Unlisted project also be archived, previously archived projects were always Public.
		- You can also include a note to explain why your project has been archived.

![In project settings, there is a new Disclosures tab. On it, you can toggle disclosures on and off, and some of them have additional fields you need to fill out.](https://modrinth.com/news/article/ai-policy-and-disclosures/settings.webp)

Projects with disclosures you’d like to avoid can be filtered out in search under the “Advanced exclusions” options. When filtering out projects with photosensitivity warnings, we will warn the user that not all projects without the warning are guaranteed to be safe for users with photosensitivities. Advanced exclusion filters will be persistent across searches in your browser so that you don't have to apply them every time you search.

![At the bottom of the search filters, there is an "Advanced exclusions" section. You can select different disclosures to exclude from your search results.](https://modrinth.com/news/article/ai-policy-and-disclosures/filters.webp)

## New AI policy

We’ve added Section 6 to the [Content Rules](https://modrinth.com/legal/rules), which is as follows:

## [6\. Usage of Generative "AI"](https://modrinth.com/legal/rules#generative-ai)

Projects must be forthright and honest about the usage of generative AI in their production, publication, and within the project itself. Projects cannot be entirely or primarily comprised of content created or derived from generative AI output.

### 6.1. Disclosure of AI generated content

You must apply the appropriate “Contains AI-generated content” content disclosure when:

1. a substantial portion of the project's code is a product of AI output.
2. the project includes any assets that are primarily or entirely a product of AI output.
3. the project's design or functionality relies on the use of generative AI.
4. any element of the project's page such as description or publishing relies on generative AI.

### 6.2. Prohibited AI generated content

1. No images uploaded to a gallery, icon, description, or any other part of a project page may be created or derived from generative AI output. Any such images may be removed.
2. Projects may not be published publicly if the contents are primarily or entirely a product of AI output.

To summarize:

- AI images as project icons, banners, gallery images, or in their descriptions are no longer allowed.
- Fully or nearly fully AI-generated projects are no longer allowed.
- AI-assisted projects, where the human creator contributed in a primary and significant way, are allowed but must disclose that AI assistance was used.

## Enforcement

Obviously, this is a big change and creators will need to take some time to update their projects to have all necessary disclosures or take down projects that are no longer allowed. For this reason, we will have a 45 day grace period to give everyone enough time to get their projects in order.

During this grace period, we will not be accepting reports for projects in violation of the new AI policy or for missing content disclosures to give them a fair chance to update them. The 45-day grace period ends on **September 27, 2026**.

In addition, we will not tolerate witch-hunting on the Modrinth platform. These disclosures are to inform users and provide transparency between user and creator. Anyone using them to shame, insult, belittle, or harass others will be swiftly and permanently removed from the Modrinth platform and community Discord server. Be kind to each other.

## Terms of Use update

Modrinth's [Terms of Use](https://modrinth.com/legal/terms) have been updated in a very minor way to prohibit the use of data on Modrinth to train AI models. The exact change is as follows:

> Additionally, you agree not to:
> 
> - \[...\]
> - Use any data, content, or materials available on or through the Service to train, develop, or improve any artificial intelligence or machine learning models.

A larger TOU update will be coming in the future to address other issues since the last update was in 2023, but we felt it was important to address this sooner rather than later.

—

Thank you for your patience with us on this feature. We know it’s been long-requested and overdue, but we wanted to make sure we shipped something comprehensive, enforceable, and more than just a publicity stunt.

Thank you as always for continuing to support us. It means a lot. 💚

Yes, check all three. Here's what each one covers in this project:

- **Code:** I wrote nearly all of it across plans 1 to 5. That includes the Java, the GameTests, the build, the workflows and the scripts.
- **Assets:** the block textures are your hand-picked ATE textures edited by a Pillow script I wrote (`~/tmp/2026-10-29-planter-textures/make_textures.py`). The logo is drawn from those textures by `tools/render_logo.py`, which I also wrote. No image generator was used, but Modrinth's rule covers any asset that is "primarily or entirely a product of AI output", and these qualify.
- **Text:** I drafted the project page, the Oracle Index guide, the README, the changelog and the in-game names and tooltips.

For the explanation box:

> I came up with the design, made the calls on how it works and tested it in game. Claude (an AI coding assistant) wrote nearly all of the code, the in-game guide and this page's text, working from my direction and review. The block textures are edits of Agritech: Evolved's hand-made textures, done by a script Claude wrote, and the mod's logo is rendered from them the same way. No image generator was used, and the screenshots are taken in game.

There's a bigger issue in the same rules. Section 6.2 says a project "may not be published publicly if the contents are primarily or entirely a product of AI output". Modrinth's guide adds a test: if a human had done the AI's part, would they count as the primary developer? For the code here, the answer is yes. Modrinth decides in review, and the guide says such projects "can still be made unlisted, but will be prohibited from appearing in public search results". Your design work and testing count in your favour, but most of the actual content came from me.

Section 6.2 also bans icons "created or derived from generative AI output". The logo was made by code I wrote, from textures my script made, so don't upload it as the Modrinth icon. A crude icon you make yourself, or no icon, is safer. The screenshots on the page come from the game itself, which the guide treats as a demonstration of in-game content.

I recommend submitting with the full disclosure above and letting Modrinth's review decide. The worst likely outcome is an unlisted project, and CurseForge and GitHub still carry the release. Don't understate the AI use to get through review: the guide says trying to get around the rules can lead to the images being removed or the account being suspended.

I found no published CurseForge rule on AI-generated mods, only a user request for one on their ideas board. If you decide to drop Modrinth, I'll clear `modrinth_project_id` so later releases skip it.
